mainTopic: Fowl and מעשר שני through כלל ופרט וכלל, and which cheap foods may be used for an ערוב
overview: The amud opens by finishing a challenge to the idea that fish are the difference between two ברייתות about what may be bought with מעשר שני money. A ברייתא about lashes for eating insects shows that water creatures are not 'on the earth.' So רבינא says the real difference is fowl. The 'גידולי קרקע' wording includes birds, and the 'ולד ולדות הארץ' wording excludes them because birds were created from mud. The גמרא explains both views through כלל ופרט וכלל. If the last כלל is the main one, a two-way resemblance is enough and fowl are included. If the first כלל is the main one, a three-way match is needed and fowl are excluded. Then the גמרא turns to ערוב: רב allows cheap plants like cress, purslane and sweet clover, but not green grain or unripe dates. The ruling on sweet clover is defended with three alternative answers, including the principle that ערוב food only needs to be fit for someone. רב's ban on green grain is reconciled with his later permission by saying he changed his view after coming to בבל. The גמרא then objects that בבל is not most of the world, and its answer begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The ברייתא about lashes for eating different insects
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that counts how many sets of מלקות one gets for eating a water insect, an ant, and a hornet.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone ate a פוטיתא (a water insect), he gets four sets of lashes. An ant: five sets. A hornet: six sets.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a ברייתא as the setup for a challenge against the earlier suggestion that fish are the difference between the two ברייתות. The challenge itself comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each creature breaks a different number of לאוין (Torah prohibitions). The פוטיתא breaks two general prohibitions about all שרצים plus two about water creatures. The ant breaks the two general ones plus three about creatures that creep on the land, and the hornet adds one more about flying creatures.

keyTerms.meaning: A small creature that lives in water
He receives מלקות (lashes)
An ant
A hornet

steps.confusionAlert: This list is not a new topic. The גמרא is only bringing it to test whether water creatures count as 'from the earth' for the מעשר שני discussion.

phrases.english: If he ate a putita (water insect), he gets four sets of lashes.
phrases.notes: Two general שרץ prohibitions plus two for water creatures.

phrases.english: An ant: he gets five sets of lashes.
phrases.notes: That's the two general prohibitions, plus three more for creatures that creep on land.

phrases.english: A hornet: he gets six sets of lashes.
phrases.notes: Adds the prohibition of flying שרצים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a challenge begun on the previous amud against the suggestion that fish are the difference between the two ברייתות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that, according to one ברייתא, fish and water creatures count as growing from the earth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only: it gives the exact count of lashes, which will be used to show that water creatures do not get the 'on the earth' prohibition.

steps.title: If water creatures were from the earth, the water insect should get more lashes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that if water creatures counted as 'from the earth,' the פוטיתא would also break the prohibition of השרץ השורץ על הארץ, so the count of four would be wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if your suggestion is right, the one who eats a פוטיתא should also get lashes because of 'every creeping thing that creeps on the earth'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge: the ברייתא gives only four lashes for the פוטיתא, which shows water creatures are not considered 'on the earth.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse 'השרץ השורץ על הארץ' applies only to creatures of the land. Since the ברייתא does not count this לאו for the water insect, water creatures are clearly not 'from the earth.' So the suggestion that fish are the difference between the ברייתות falls.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it were so (if your claim were correct)
He should receive lashes
'The creeping thing that creeps on the earth' (ויקרא יא:מא)

steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge knocks out the fish explanation and forces the גמרא to look for a new difference between the ברייתות.

phrases.english: And if it is so (that water creatures count as from the earth),
the putita should also bring lashes
phrases.notes: An extra set beyond the four.

phrases.english: because of 'the creeping thing that creeps on the earth'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the ברייתא from step 1 to attack the fish explanation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that fish count as גידולי קרקע or ולד ולדות הארץ according to one of the ברייתות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If water creatures counted as from the earth, the פוטיתא would also break the 'on the earth' לאו and get five lashes. The ברייתא says four, so water creatures are not from the earth.

steps.title: רבינא: the difference between the two ברייתות is fowl
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives a new answer: the two ברייתות disagree about fowl. One counts them as growing from the ground, and the other says they were created from mud.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבינא said: the difference between them is fowl. The one who says 'produce of produce and grown from the ground' holds that fowl also count as grown from the ground. The one who says 'offspring of the offspring of the earth' holds that fowl were created from mud, so they are excluded.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the fish explanation fell, רבינא offers a different practical difference between the two ברייתות: whether you may buy birds with מעשר שני money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the wording גידולי קרקע, birds are also considered grown from the ground. Under the wording ולד ולדות הארץ, birds do not count, because birds were created from רקק (swampy mud), as חז"ל derive from the creation verses, and not from the earth itself. So the same birds are included by one wording and excluded by the other.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (the earlier answer is dropped and a new one is given)
An אמורא who gives the new answer
There is a difference between them
Produce from produce, and grown from the ground
Offspring of the offspring of the earth
Swampy mud from which birds were created

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the direction: the 'גידולי קרקע' ברייתא INCLUDES fowl, and the 'ולד ולדות הארץ' ברייתא EXCLUDES fowl. It is easy to mix them up.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rest of the סוגיא, which explains each side's reasoning about fowl using the rules of כלל ופרט.

phrases.english: Rather, Ravina said:
Fowl is the difference between them.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר פְּרִי מִפְּרִי וְגִידּוּלֵי קַרְקַע,
phrases.english: According to the one who says 'produce of produce and grown from the ground,'
these (fowl) are also grown from the ground.
phrases.notes: Birds are nourished by what grows from the ground.

phrases.english: According to the one who says 'offspring of the offspring of the earth,'
these fowl were created from mud.
phrases.notes: So they are not 'of the earth' and are excluded.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the fish explanation, which was refuted in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New identification of the practical difference (נפקא מינה) between the two ברייתות
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the two ברייתות disagree about fish.
steps.terutzMaskana: They disagree about fowl: the גידולי קרקע wording includes birds, and the ולד ולדות הארץ wording excludes them because birds came from mud.

steps.title: What is each side's reason about fowl?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind including fowl and behind excluding them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who includes fowl, what is his reason? And the one who excludes fowl, what is his reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move: it asks for the source-based reasoning of each side, which it will explain next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides learn from the same פסוק about מעשר שני, which has the structure of כלל ופרט וכלל. So the גמרא wants to know how one פסוק can lead to two different results about fowl.

keyTerms.meaning: Includes
Excludes
What is his reason?

phrases.english: The one who includes fowl, what is his reason,
and the one who excludes fowl, what is his reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רבינא's two positions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exegetical basis for including or excluding fowl from מעשר שני purchases.

steps.title: The reason of the one who includes fowl: the last generalization decides
steps.stepSummary: The one who includes fowl holds that in a כלל ופרט וכלל, the last כלל is the main one, so almost everything is included. The first כלל only excludes things that do not resemble the details in two ways.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who includes fowl holds that the last generalization is the one that counts. It works like 'a detail and then a generalization,' where the generalization adds to the detail and everything is included. But the first generalization still does something: it excludes anything that does not resemble the detail in two respects.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the first half of the question: it explains why one opinion includes fowl. The reason of the other opinion comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about מעשר שני has a כלל ('whatever your soul desires'), a פרט ('cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink'), and another כלל ('whatever your soul asks of you'). This opinion treats the final כלל as decisive, like פרט וכלל, which widens the list to almost everything. The first כלל keeps only a small limit: an item must match the details in two respects (פרי מפרי and גידולי קרקע), and anything that does not match in both is excluded. Fowl match in both, so they are included.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds
The last generalization is the decisive one
A detail followed by a generalization
The generalization adds to the detail (widening it)
The first generalization
In two respects

steps.confusionAlert: The standard rule of כלל ופרט וכלל is 'only things like the פרט.' This opinion is wider, because a resemblance in two respects is enough and a full three-way match is not needed. But an item must still match in BOTH of those two respects. Matching in just one is not enough.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how one פסוק can be read broadly or narrowly. The next step will give the narrower reading that excludes fowl.

phrases.english: The one who includes fowl holds:
The latter generalization is decisive.
A detail and a generalization:
the generalization becomes an addition to the detail,
and all things are included.
And the first generalization is effective
phrases.notes: It still has some limiting effect.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַעוֹטֵי כֹּל דְּלָא דָּמֵי לֵיהּ מִשְּׁנֵי צְדָדִין.
phrases.english: to exclude anything that does not resemble it in two respects.
phrases.notes: The two respects are fruit from fruit (פרי מפרי) and growing from the ground (גידולי קרקע); fowl have both.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first half of the question in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The includer reads the פסוק as mainly a broad פרט וכלל because the final כלל is decisive. The first כלל excludes only items that do not resemble the פרט in two respects (פרי מפרי and גידולי קרקע). Fowl have both, so they are included.

steps.title: The reasoning of the view that excludes fowl
steps.stepSummary: The one who excludes fowl holds that the first כלל is the main one. So the last כלל only adds things that resemble the details in three ways, and fowl fail that test.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who excludes fowl holds that the first כלל is the main one. A כלל followed by a פרט includes only what the פרט lists: those items, yes, and anything else, no. The last כלל is still useful, because it adds anything that resembles the details in three ways.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes answering the question from Step 4. It now explains the side that excludes fowl.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 explained the side that treats the last כלל as the main one, which gives a wide inclusion that only needs a two-way resemblance. This step flips that. If the first כלל is the main one, we start from a narrow list, and the last כלל adds only things that match the details in all three ways (פרי מפרי, growing from the ground, and offspring of the earth's offspring). Fowl do not match in every way, so they are excluded.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who excludes
The first generalization
Precise, the main one that sets the rule
A general statement followed by a specific list. Only the listed items are included.
In three respects

steps.whatToRemember: Both views use the same כלל ופרט וכלל. The disagreement is which כלל is the main one. If the last כלל is the main one, a two-way resemblance is enough and fowl are included. If the first כלל is the main one, a three-way resemblance is needed and fowl are excluded.
steps.confusionAlert: Even the view that excludes fowl does not say the last כלל adds nothing. It still adds things, but only those that match the details in all three ways.

phrases.english: And the one who excludes fowl
holds: the first generalization is the main one,
so it is like a generalization followed by a detail,
and the generalization includes only what is in the detail:
these items, yes; anything else, no.
But the last generalization is effective

phrases.aramaic: לְרַבּוֹיֵי כֹּל דְּדָמֵי לֵיהּ מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה צְדָדִין.
phrases.english: to include anything that resembles it in three respects.
phrases.notes: The three respects are: fruit from fruit, growing from the ground, and offspring of the earth's offspring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-part answer begun in Step 5 by giving the opposite side's reasoning.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does one ברייתא exclude fowl?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because it treats the first כלל as the main one, so only items that resemble the details in all three ways are included, and fowl do not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes רבינא's answer. The two ברייתות are now fully explained as a dispute about how to read a כלל ופרט וכלל.

steps.title: Cheap plants that may and may not be used for an ערוב
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that an ערוב may be made with פעפועין, חלגלוגות, and גודגדניות, but not with חזיז or כפניות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב שמואל בר שילת, who said it in the name of רב: You may make an ערוב with cress, purslane, and sweet clover, but not with green grain or unripe dates.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new statement about which foods can be used for an ערוב. רב lists some cheap plants that are allowed and two that are not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ערוב must be made with food. רב teaches that even cheap, humble plants count as food for this purpose. חזיז (grain still green) and כפניות (unripe dates) do not count, because people do not normally eat them as they are.

keyTerms.meaning: You may make an ערוב
Cress, a cheap edible plant
Purslane
Sweet clover
Grain that is still green, used as animal fodder
Unripe dates

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat
in the name of Rav:
One may make an eiruv with cress
and with purslane and with sweet clover,
but not with green grain and not with unripe dates.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: specific foods that are valid for an ערוב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cheap plants such as פעפועין, חלגלוגות, and גודגדניות are valid for an ערוב. חזיז and כפניות are not.

steps.title: Challenge: sweet clover is not food for everyone
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says people without children may not eat גודגדניות, and once hardened into seed no one may eat them. So how can רב allow an ערוב with them?
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really make an ערוב with sweet clover? A ברייתא teaches about sweet clover that people with many children may eat it and people without children may not. If it has hardened into seed, even people with many children may not eat it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling about גודגדניות by quoting a ברייתא that limits who may eat them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ערוב must be made with food that is fit to eat. The ברייתא shows that גודגדניות are harmful to some people, because they hurt fertility, and once hardened they are harmful to everyone. That seems to contradict רב's broad permission.

keyTerms.meaning: But was it not taught in a ברייתא?
People who have many children
People who have no children
Hardened into seed, fully hard and ready to plant

phrases.english: And may one really make an eiruv with sweet clover?
But it was taught in a baraita: sweet clover —
those with many children may eat it,
those without children may not eat it,
and if it hardened into seed,
even those with many children may not eat it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks one item in רב's list from Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's permission to make an ערוב with גודגדניות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An ערוב requires edible food. A ברייתא shows גודגדניות are forbidden to some people, and when hardened they are forbidden to everyone. So they seem invalid for an ערוב.

steps.title: Answer: unhardened clover, for people with many children
steps.stepSummary: רב's ruling is limited to גודגדניות that have not hardened into seed, used by people who have many children.
steps.simpleTranslation: Explain רב's ruling as talking about sweet clover that has not hardened into seed, and about people who have many children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing רב's ruling to the case where the ברייתא allows eating the clover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not reject the ברייתא. It narrows רב's case to fit it. רב's permission applies only where the clover is fit to eat: before it hardens, and for someone with many children.

keyTerms.meaning: Interpret it, explain it as referring to a specific case

steps.whatToRemember: According to this first answer, רב's permission is limited: גודגדניות work only before they harden, and only for someone with many children. The next step gives a different answer that drops the second limit.

phrases.english: Interpret it as referring to clover that did not harden into seed,
and to those with many children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge from Step 8 by limiting רב's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב allowed an ערוב with any גודגדניות, for anyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב allowed it only with unhardened גודגדניות, for people with many children, who are allowed to eat them.

steps.title: Clover works even for people without children
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: רב's ruling about גודגדניות applies even to people without children, because the clover is fit for people with many children.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say this: really, רב allows it even for people without children, because the clover is fit for people who have many children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new answer to the question from Step 8. It says רב did not need to limit his ruling to people with many children after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 limited רב's ruling to people with many children. This answer removes that limit. Food for an ערוב does not have to be edible for the person making it, as long as it is fit for other people.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you prefer, say (introduces another answer)
Really / actually (keeping the original case)
People without children
People with many children

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new question. It is a second, different answer to the same question from Step 8. It is offered as an alternative to the answer in Step 9 (ואיבעית אימא), not a rejection of it.

phrases.english: And if you prefer, say:
Really, it works even for people without children,
since it is fit for people with many children.
phrases.notes: The food only has to be edible for someone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to Step 8 instead of the limit set in Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Broader principle: food for an ערוב only needs to be fit for some people
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The questioner assumed the food must be edible for the person making the ערוב.
steps.terutzMaskana: Food fit for any group of people works for everyone, so even people without children may use clover.

steps.title: Proof from a נזיר and תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves the principle from a משנה: an ערוב may be made for a נזיר with wine and for a non-כהן with תרומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did we not learn in a משנה: We may make an ערוב for a נזיר with wine, and for a regular Jew with תרומה? This shows that even though the food is not fit for this person, it is fit for that person. Here too, even though the clover is not fit for this person, it is fit for that person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof for the answer it just gave in Step 10. It points to a משנה where food that the person cannot eat still works for an ערוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נזיר may not drink wine, and a regular Jew may not eat תרומה, yet the משנה lets them use these foods for an ערוב. The reason is that other people (non-נזירים, כהנים) can eat them. The same logic applies to clover: if people with many children can eat it, it works for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: Did we not learn in a משנה?
A person who took a vow not to drink wine
Food given to a כהן, forbidden to others
This shows that
It is fit for this one

steps.whatToRemember: Food for an ערוב only needs to be fit for some people, not necessarily for the person making it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle explains many cases in the laws of ערוב, where the food counts as long as it is real food for someone.

phrases.english: Did we not learn in a Mishnah:
We may make an eruv for a nazir with wine,
and for a regular Jew with teruma.

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא חֲזֵי לְהַאי —
phrases.english: This shows: even though it is not fit for this one,
it is fit for that one.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי, אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא חֲזֵי לְהַאי —
phrases.english: Here too, even though it is not fit for this one,
it is fit for that one.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי לָא תְּנַן: מְעָרְבִין לַנָּזִיר בְּיַיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of Step 10 with a source.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that food for an ערוב only needs to be fit for someone
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה allowing wine for a נזיר and תרומה for a regular Jew

steps.title: רב meant the clover from Media
steps.stepSummary: A third answer: רב was talking about a special kind of clover from Media, which is not harmful.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say this: when רב said it, he meant Median clover.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer to the question from Step 8. It says רב was talking about a different type of clover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in Step 8 warned against eating clover. This answer says that ברייתא was about regular clover, but רב meant a better kind from Media that does not cause harm. So there is no contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: When he said it
Median clover, a better and harmless kind

phrases.english: And if you prefer, say:
When Rav said it,
he was talking about Median clover.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Different case: a different kind of clover
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's clover is the same harmful clover the ברייתא talks about.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב meant Median clover, which is safe to eat.

steps.title: רב also allowed green grain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling that חזיז may not be used, since רב יהודה quotes רב as allowing חזיז for an ערוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And with green grain we may not make an ערוב? But רב יהודה said in the name of רב: With dodder and green grain we may make an ערוב, and we say the blessing 'בורא פרי האדמה' on them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves to the second part of רב's ruling from Step 7 and challenges it. It shows that רב seems to contradict himself about חזיז.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 7, רב said an ערוב may not be made with חזיז. But רב יהודה quotes רב saying it may be used, and that it gets the blessing of vegetables. Two statements from the same רב seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: Green grain (grain picked before it ripens)
Dodder, a plant eaten as food
But did he not say? (introduces a contradiction)
Blessing on foods that grow from the ground

phrases.english: And with green grain we may not?
But Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
Dodder and green grain, we may make an eruv with them,
and we say on them the blessing 'Who creates the fruit of the ground'!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבַחֲזִיז לָא? וְהָאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from גודגדניות to the next item in רב's list, חזיז.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling in Step 7 that חזיז may not be used for an ערוב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב is quoted elsewhere as allowing חזיז, so his two statements contradict each other.

steps.title: רב changed his ruling after coming to בבל
steps.stepSummary: The answer: one ruling was said before רב came to בבל, and the other after he came, when he saw people there eat green grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not a problem. This ruling was said before רב came to בבל, and that ruling was said after רב came to בבל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction from Step 13. It says רב said the two rulings at different times in his life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before coming to בבל, רב did not consider green grain real food, so he did not allow it for an ערוב. After he came to בבל and saw people eating it, he treated it as food and allowed it. Since ערוב food depends on what people actually eat, the ruling changed with the place.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not a problem
Before he came
After he came
Babylonia

steps.whatToRemember: Whether something counts as food for an ערוב can depend on local eating habits. רב allowed חזיז once he saw people in בבל eat it.

phrases.english: It is not a problem:
This one was before Rav came to Babylonia,
that one was after Rav came to Babylonia.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא מִקַּמֵּי דַּאֲתָא רַב לְבָבֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different times: רב changed his ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both rulings were said at the same time and contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban came before רב reached בבל; the permission came after, once he saw green grain eaten there.

steps.title: בבל is not most of the world
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב could base a ruling on the eating habits of בבל, since הלכה follows the custom of most of the world. It brings a ברייתא about מעשרות as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is בבל the majority of the world? It was taught in a ברייתא: beans, barley and fenugreek that someone planted to use as greens — his intention is cancelled by what all other people do. So the seeds must be tithed and the greens are exempt. Cress and arugula planted for greens are tithed as greens and as seeds. If planted for seeds, they are tithed as seeds and as greens.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 14. That answer said רב allowed green grain because people in בבל eat it. The problem is that בבל is only one place, and הלכה goes by what most people in the world do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא teaches that if one person plants beans, barley or fenugreek to eat as greens, his unusual plan is ignored, because most people do not eat them that way. The greens are therefore exempt from מעשר. In the same way, the local habit of בבל should be cancelled by the rest of the world, so green grain should not count as normal food for an ערוב.

keyTerms.meaning: The majority of the world; what most people everywhere do
But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא? (introduces a source used to challenge)
His intention is cancelled by what all other people do
Fenugreek, a plant normally grown for its seeds
Cress and arugula, plants commonly eaten both as greens and as seeds
They must be tithed (have מעשר taken)

steps.confusionAlert: Only the first half of the ברייתא (beans, barley, fenugreek) is the real proof. The cress and arugula part is quoted because it is part of the same ברייתא. It shows the contrast: when people commonly eat a plant both ways, both forms are tithed. Don't look for the main proof there.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out a basic rule found all over ש"ס: הלכה about what counts as 'food' or 'normal use' follows the majority of people, not the habits of one individual or one place.

phrases.english: And is Babylonia the majority of the world?
phrases.notes: He's asking this to make a point: Babylonia is NOT most of the world.

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught in a baraita:
Beans, barley, and fenugreek
that one planted to use as greens —
phrases.notes: For example, as animal feed, before the seeds ripen.

phrases.english: his intention is cancelled by that of all other people.
phrases.notes: This is the key line for the challenge.

phrases.english: Therefore: their seeds are obligated in tithes,
and their greens are exempt.
phrases.notes: The greens are not treated as a finished crop.

phrases.english: Cress and arugula that one planted for greens —
are tithed as greens and as seeds,
if one planted them for seeds — they are tithed as seeds and as greens.
phrases.notes: People commonly eat these plants both ways, so both forms are tithed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation in step 14, which said רב's lenient ruling came from seeing Babylonians eat green grain.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer from step 14: רב allowed חזיז for an ערוב because people in בבל eat green grain.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The halachic status of food follows the majority of the world (בטלה דעתו אצל כל אדם). בבל is a minority, so its local habit should not make green grain count as food.
